newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-BIL not wanting control of Coles.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-BIL not wanting control of Coles.

text.p: Brierley Investments Ltd is comfortable with its 6.8 percent stake in Coles Myer and has no intention of seeking control of the giant Australian retailer, BIL chairman Bob Matthew said on Wednesday.
"We don't envisage us or anyone else obtaining control. We are not going to buy it. It is not probable that we are going to acquire the business," Matthew said in an interview.
"We are comfortable with our present stake."
BIL's foray over the last year into Coles, which has been beset by management and board strife, has had analysts and media commentators working overtime trying to assess BIL's intentions.
The media has speculated that BIL could be working with its 20 percent shareholder, the Delham consortium, a grouping of five of the most powerful business names in Southeast Asia.
Despite BIL having a warchest of around NZ$1.5 billion, Coles with a capitalisation of around A$5 billion was too big even for BIL.
But Matthew made it clear BIL was not tagging along for the ride and would be active in straightening Coles out.
"You can take it that we would not be the only significant shareholder prepared to face up to whatever it is the business should be doing," Matthew said.
But he stressed BIL was independent.
"We are our own men. We have no promises or obligations to others and we are now equipped to participate in judgments that that company takes as to what will, and how it will, enhance value."
Any action BIL effected would be via the board. Any apparent circumspection about what BIL said was not because it did not know what to do but because it did not wish to reveal its hand.
"We are not passive shareholders," he said.
BIL's Chief Executive Paul Collins has been granted a place on the Coles board but some analysts doubt one board place is enough influence.
Matthew was coy on BIL's relationship with 14 percent Coles shareholder Solomon Lew, around whom much of the controversy in the company has centred.
Matthew, who has never met Lew, would say little about him but noted they are shareholders with a common goal to maximise value in Coles. He hinted at areas of cooperation.
"We certainly haven't bought on the quaint notion that it represents something more than 15 cents spent in every dollar spent in Australia so there's got to be a quid in it."
Matthew noted that institutions had deserted Coles after playing an unusually active role trying to change Coles.

"The institutions chose to be in the forefront of change which was unusual for them, and it could be said to have been usual for them to have taken those initiatives and then left the stock," he said.
Collins recently suggested to analysts that the institutions which sold stock to BIL may be buying it back in a few years at a much higher price.
Matthew said BIL had initially been deeply criticised for recent similar plays in publisher Wilson & Horton and building products company James Hardie but had been vindicated.
BIL remains confident of a repeat performance but Matthew rejects one analyst's comment that this was a credibility issue for BIL as it seeks to get more involved in Australia.
He said everything BIL did was a credibility issue but the Coles play repesented only NZ$400 million out of assets of NZ$7 billion and was no more material than any other play.
However, he welcomes the intense interest in Coles.
"The interest that exists in BIL's role might well suit BIL well. It tends to be productive to be an investor in a company in which everyone is interested.
"Perhaps some of this interest is due to the observers themselves not knowing what they should be doing."
